subject: ela
intro: Grade 6 grammar focuses on four key areas: pronoun case (subjective, objective, and possessive), intensive pronouns (myself, himself, herself), vague pronoun reference (making sure every pronoun clearly refers to a specific noun), and subject-verb agreement (especially with tricky subjects like collective nouns and indefinite pronouns).

items.prompt:
Choose the correct pronoun form:

'The winners of the competition were (she / her) and (I / me).'

Explain how to determine which form is correct.

steps: After the linking verb 'were,' use subjective pronouns because the subject and predicate refer to the same thing.
'She' is subjective; 'her' is objective. 'I' is subjective; 'me' is objective.
Test: 'The winner was she' — not 'her.'
Test: 'The winner was I' — not 'me.'
solution.answer: Correct: 'The winners of the competition were she and I.' Both pronouns follow a linking verb, so they must be in the subjective case. A quick test: replace each pronoun alone: 'The winner was she' and 'The winner was I' both sound correct in formal English. 'The winner was her/me' would be incorrect.

items.prompt:
Identify the error in this sentence and correct it:

'Give the permission slip to Maria and I.'

steps: 'To' is a preposition. Pronouns after prepositions must be in the objective case.
Objective pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.
Test: remove 'Maria and' — 'Give the permission slip to I' sounds clearly wrong.
Correct: 'Give the permission slip to me.'
solution.answer: Error: 'I' should be 'me.' The pronoun follows the preposition 'to,' which requires the objective case. Test: remove the other noun ('Maria and') and say the sentence: 'Give the permission slip to I' is obviously wrong. Corrected: 'Give the permission slip to Maria and me.'

items.prompt:
What is an intensive pronoun? Identify one in this sentence and explain its function:

'The principal herself announced the school's new schedule.'

steps: Intensive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) emphasize a noun or pronoun already in the sentence.
Here, 'herself' emphasizes 'the principal' — the principal did it personally, no one else.
Remove the pronoun: the sentence still makes sense grammatically. That confirms it is intensive (not reflexive).
solution.answer: 'Herself' is an intensive pronoun. It emphasizes that the principal personally made the announcement, not a vice principal or other representative. You can remove it without changing the basic meaning: 'The principal announced the schedule' is still grammatically complete. The intensive pronoun adds emphasis, not grammatical function.

items.prompt:
Find the vague pronoun reference and rewrite the sentence to fix it:

'Maya called Keisha when she arrived at the party.'

steps: The pronoun 'she' is ambiguous: it could refer to Maya or Keisha.
Who arrived at the party — Maya or Keisha?
Rewrite by replacing the pronoun with the specific noun.
solution.answer: The pronoun 'she' is vague because it could refer to either Maya or Keisha. Fix by specifying: 'Maya called Keisha when Maya arrived at the party.' OR 'Maya called Keisha when Keisha arrived at the party.' The choice depends on who actually arrived; the sentence must make it unambiguous.

items.prompt:
Choose the correct verb form:

'The team (is / are) celebrating their victory.'

Explain your reasoning.

steps: 'Team' is a collective noun: it refers to a group acting together.
In American English, collective nouns (team, committee, jury, class) are treated as singular when acting as a unit.
The team is acting together (celebrating together), so use singular 'is.'
solution.answer: Correct: 'The team is celebrating their victory.' In American English, collective nouns like 'team' take singular verbs when the group acts as a unit. Because the team is celebrating together (not each member separately), 'is' is correct. Note: the pronoun 'their' can refer to the group in modern usage even with the singular verb.

items.prompt:
Choose the correct pronoun and explain your reasoning:

(A) '(Who / Whom) did the teacher choose to present first?'
(B) '(We / Us) students organized the fundraiser ourselves.'
items.hint: For (A): substitute he/him. For (B): try the sentence without 'students.'

steps: (A) Substitute he/him: 'The teacher chose him.' 'Him' = objective, so use 'whom.'
(B) Remove 'students': 'Us organized the fundraiser' vs 'We organized the fundraiser.' 'We' is clearly correct (subjective).
solution.answer: (A) 'Whom' — the pronoun is the object of 'choose.' Test: 'The teacher chose him/whom.' Since 'him' is correct (objective), use 'whom.' (B) 'We' — the pronoun is the subject. Test: remove 'students' to isolate the pronoun: 'We organized the fundraiser' is correct. 'Us organized' is not.

items.prompt:
Correct the pronoun error in each sentence:

(A) 'The coach gave the trophy to he and Jamal.'
(B) 'Between you and I, I think we should study more.'
items.hint: Both errors involve pronouns following prepositions.

steps: (A) 'to' is a preposition, so objective case: 'him.'
(B) 'between' is a preposition, so objective case: 'me.'
solution.answer: (A) 'The coach gave the trophy to him and Jamal.' (Test: 'gave it to he' is wrong; 'gave it to him' is correct.) (B) 'Between you and me, I think we should study more.' ('Between you and I' is a very common error; 'between' is a preposition requiring the objective 'me.')

items.prompt:
Fix the vague pronoun reference:

'When David met his father at the airport, he was exhausted from the long flight.'
items.hint: Ask yourself: who was exhausted from the long flight, David or his father?

steps: 'He' could refer to David or his father.
Decide who was exhausted and rewrite accordingly.
solution.answer: If David was exhausted: 'When David met his father at the airport, David was exhausted from the long flight.' If the father was exhausted: 'When David met his father at the airport, his father was exhausted from the long flight.' The fix is to replace the ambiguous pronoun with the specific noun.

items.prompt:
Choose the correct verb for the indefinite pronoun subjects:

(A) 'Neither of the students (has / have) finished the test.'
(B) 'Each of the animals (needs / need) individual care.'
items.hint: Indefinite pronouns like 'neither' and 'each' are typically singular.

steps: 'Neither' is singular, even though it refers to more than one person.
'Each' is singular by definition (one at a time).
solution.answer: (A) 'Neither of the students has finished.' 'Neither' is a singular indefinite pronoun. (B) 'Each of the animals needs individual care.' 'Each' is always singular. Both sentences follow the rule that singular indefinite pronouns (each, every, either, neither, anyone, nobody, etc.) take singular verbs.

items.prompt:
Identify whether each sentence uses an intensive pronoun correctly, incorrectly, or not at all:

(A) 'I myself completed the entire experiment alone.'
(B) 'Me and myself will handle the presentation.'
(C) 'The students themselves designed the mural.'
items.hint: An intensive pronoun emphasizes a noun already in the sentence. It is never used as a subject.

steps: (A) 'myself' emphasizes 'I' — this is a correct intensive pronoun use.
(B) 'myself' is used as a subject alongside 'me,' which is also wrong. 'Me and myself' should be 'I myself.'
(C) 'themselves' emphasizes 'the students' — correct intensive use.
solution.answer: (A) Correct intensive pronoun use. 'Myself' emphasizes that I, not anyone else, completed the experiment. (B) Incorrect. 'Myself' cannot be used as a subject. Corrected: 'I myself will handle the presentation.' (C) Correct. 'Themselves' emphasizes the students' direct involvement in designing the mural.
